title: 22. Interview: Grafana
summary: Interview Q&A for Grafana — 14 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 14 Grafana interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Conceptual Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. What is Grafana's data source abstraction, and why is it the key to Grafana's success?
**Answer:** Grafana itself stores no data — it is a query engine and renderer. Every panel is configured with a data source (a connection to a database) and a query in that database's native query language (PromQL for Prometheus, LogQL for Loki, SQL for MySQL, Lucene for Elasticsearch). When a user opens a dashboard, Grafana fans out the queries to all configured data sources in parallel, receives responses in each source's native format, normalizes them into a common data frame (time + value columns + metadata), and renders them as panels. This abstraction is the key to Grafana's success because it lets one tool serve the entire observability stack: a single dashboard can show a Prometheus metric chart, a Loki log stream, and a MySQL table side by side, with cross-panel linking. Without this abstraction, a team would need Kibana for Elasticsearch, a separate UI for Prometheus, a separate UI for CloudWatch — Grafana unifies them. The trade-off is that Grafana cannot use any feature the data source does not expose, so its panels are constrained by the underlying query languages.

**Visual:**
```
Grafana (no data):
  panel 1 -> PromQL -> Prometheus
  panel 2 -> LogQL  -> Loki
  panel 3 -> SQL    -> MySQL
  panel 4 -> Lucene -> Elasticsearch
  all rendered in one dashboard, cross-linked

vs. without Grafana: 4 separate UIs, no cross-linking
```

### Q2. What are Grafana templating variables, and why are they essential for dashboard maintainability?
**Answer:** Templating variables are drop-down selectors at the top of a dashboard that filter every panel's query. A variable like `$service` is defined as a query (`label_values(http_requests_total, service)` in Prometheus) that returns the list of distinct values; the variable's current value is substituted into every panel's query (`http_requests_total{service="$service"}`). Variables can be chained — `$region` filters `$cluster` filters `$instance` — so selecting "us-east-1" populates the second dropdown with only us-east-1 clusters. They are essential for maintainability because without them, a team ends up with one dashboard per service per environment (a 50-service, 3-environment company would have 150 nearly-identical dashboards), which is unmaintainable. With variables, one dashboard template serves all of them, and the team maintains one source of truth. Variables also include text-box variables (free-form filters), interval variables (used in `rate(...[$__interval])` for auto-binned rates based on the dashboard time range), and custom constants. The discipline is to use variables for everything that varies across deployments: environment, region, cluster, service, instance, route.

**Visual:**
```
Without variables:  checkout-prod-us1.md, checkout-prod-eu1.md, ...
                     50 services x 3 envs x 3 regions = 450 dashboards

With variables:     1 dashboard with [$service] [$env] [$region]
                    selector populates from label_values()
                    -> 1 source of truth, 450 use cases
```

### Q3. Explain Grafana's panel types and when to use each.
**Answer:** Time series is the default for metric-over-time data — line charts with multiple series, used for latency, throughput, error rate. Stat shows a single large number with optional sparkline — used for KPI tiles at the top of dashboards ("current p99 latency: 245ms"). Gauge shows a single value on a dial with thresholds — used for utilization metrics ("CPU: 73%, threshold 80%"). Table renders rows and columns — used for non-time-series data like top-N queries or inventory lists. Heatmap shows a 2D distribution (e.g., latency bucket over time) — used for latency distributions where p50/p90/p99 alone hide the shape. Logs (Loki-specific) renders a stream of log lines with syntax highlighting and label filtering — used for log forensics. Node graph renders a directed graph of nodes and edges — used for service meshes and trace topologies. Geomap renders points on a map — used for geographic distributions (CDN edge traffic, regional outages). Bar chart renders categorical comparisons — used for cross-service comparisons. The discipline is to pick the panel type that answers the question: "is the service healthy?" -> stat tiles + time series; "why is it slow?" -> heatmap of latency + logs; "what's the topology?" -> node graph.

**Visual:**
```
Question              -> Panel type
"is it healthy?"      -> stat (KPI tiles)
"latency over time?"  -> timeseries (line chart)
"latency distribution?" -> heatmap (2D: bucket x time)
"top errors?"         -> table (sortable rows)
"why slow?"           -> timeseries + logs (correlated)
"topology?"           -> node graph (service mesh)
"regional traffic?"   -> geomap (lat/long points)
```

### Q4. How does Grafana provisioning work, and why is it the production-grade way to manage dashboards?
**Answer:** Grafana stores dashboards, data sources, alert rules, and notification policies in its database by default — but for production reliability, this state should be in version control. Grafana's provisioning system lets teams define these resources as YAML files in directories (`/etc/grafana/provisioning/dashboards/`, `/etc/grafana/provisioning/datasources/`, `/etc/grafana/provisioning/alerting/`), and Grafana loads them on startup, reconciling the database state to match the files. Files in the provisioning directories are treated as the source of truth — changes made in the Grafana UI to provisioned dashboards are not persisted (the dashboard reverts on next reload), preventing drift. This enables GitOps workflows: dashboards live in a Git repo, pull requests review dashboard changes, CI/CD deploys the repo to the Grafana instance, and the dashboard state is reproducible from source. The Terraform provider and `grafana-cli` extend this to manage dashboards, data sources, folders, teams, and permissions as code. The discipline is: never edit dashboards in production directly — always edit in a staging instance, export to JSON, commit to Git, deploy via provisioning. This is the same pattern as infrastructure-as-code, applied to observability.

**Visual:**
```
Without provisioning:
  engineer edits dashboard in UI -> saved to DB
  -> no version control, no review, no rollback
  -> dashboard drift, stale panels, no audit trail

With provisioning (GitOps):
  dashboards/*.yaml in Git -> PR review -> CI deploy
  -> /etc/grafana/provisioning/dashboards/
  -> Grafana loads on startup, reconciles DB
  -> versioned, reviewed, rollback via git revert
```

### Q5. How does Grafana alerting differ from Prometheus alerting, and when do you use each?
**Answer:** Grafana alerting, introduced in v8 (2021) and unified in v9, lets users define alert rules that query any data source (Prometheus, Loki, MySQL, CloudWatch), evaluate on a schedule, and route to notification channels. Prometheus alerting is built into Prometheus itself: alert rules are written in PromQL, evaluated by Prometheus, and routed to Alertmanager for dedup, grouping, and notification. The key differences: Grafana alerting can alert on any data source (cross-source alerts like "Loki log error rate exceeds threshold" or "MySQL query returned anomaly"), while Prometheus alerting is limited to Prometheus metrics. Grafana alerting has a unified UI and a contact-points/policies model that handles routing, silencing, and inhibition within Grafana, while Prometheus uses Alertmanager as a separate component. Grafana alerting's state is stored in the Grafana database (or provisioned as YAML), while Prometheus alert rules are stored in Prometheus config. The common pattern is: use Prometheus alerting for metric-based alerts (integrates with Alertmanager's mature dedup/grouping), use Grafana alerting for cross-source alerts (logs, SQL, CloudWatch) that Prometheus cannot express. Some teams use one or the other exclusively to avoid managing two alerting systems.

**Visual:**
```
Prometheus alerting:  PromQL rule -> Prom evaluates -> Alertmanager
                      (metrics only, mature dedup/grouping)

Grafana alerting:     any query -> Grafana evaluates -> Grafana routes
                      (logs, SQL, CloudWatch, cross-source)

Typical split:
  metric alerts      -> Prometheus + Alertmanager
  log/SQL/cross-src  -> Grafana alerting
```

### Q6. What is the Grafana Stack (Loki, Tempo, Mimir), and how does it compare to Datadog?
**Answer:** The Grafana Stack is Grafana Labs' companion products that integrate tightly with Grafana: Loki (log aggregation, designed for label-based queries like Prometheus but for logs — it indexes only labels, not full text, so it is 10–100x cheaper than Elasticsearch), Tempo (distributed tracing backend, native OpenTelemetry support, stores traces in object storage), Mimir (horizontally-scalable Prometheus-compatible metrics backend, the successor to Cortex, designed for multi-tenant planetary-scale metrics), OnCall (pager and on-call schedule management, an alternative to PagerDuty), Alloy (OpenTelemetry-compatible collector). The integration is the value: a Grafana dashboard can show a Prometheus metric chart, click a point to see the Loki logs from that time window for that service, click a log line to see the Tempo trace for that request ID, and click a span in the trace to see the relevant logs — the "three pillars in one UI" workflow. Versus Datadog, the trade-off is: Datadog is a single-vendor SaaS with tight integration but per-host pricing that gets expensive at scale (a 1,000-host deployment can be $200K+/year); the Grafana Stack is open-source, self-hostable, and uses commodity object storage, so the marginal cost of a new host is near zero, but the team must operate the stack. For teams that want full control and have the operational capacity, Grafana Stack is the answer; for teams that want zero-ops observability, Datadog wins.

**Visual:**
```
Grafana Stack (self-hosted, open-source):
  Mimir (metrics) + Loki (logs) + Tempo (traces) + Grafana (UI)
  + OnCall (paging) + Alloy (collector)
  cost: ~$0 marginal per host (commodity S3)
  ops:  team runs the stack

Datadog (SaaS, single vendor):
  metrics + logs + traces + APM in one product
  cost: ~$15-30/host/month -> $200K+/yr at 1000 hosts
  ops:  Datadog runs it, you send data
```

### Q7. How do you design a "golden signals" dashboard, and why is it the canonical SRE dashboard?
**Answer:** The golden signals dashboard, based on Google SRE's "four golden signals" (latency, traffic, errors, saturation), is the canonical SRE dashboard because it answers the single most important operational question — "is the service healthy, and if not, where is the problem?" — in one screen. The design is: top row is four stat tiles showing current values of the four signals (latency p99, requests-per-second, error rate, CPU utilization) with thresholds color-coded green/yellow/red so the engineer can assess health in one glance. Middle rows are time-series charts of the same four signals over the last hour, so the engineer can see trends and spot the moment a metric started deviating. Bottom row is a log panel filtered to errors only, so the engineer can immediately see what the service is logging when it is failing. Templating variables (`$service`, `$env`, `$region`) make the same dashboard serve every service. The dashboard is the entry point for incident response: the alert fires, the engineer opens the golden dashboard, sees which signal is red, drills into the time-series chart to see when it started, and reads the error logs to see what failed. From there, the engineer navigates to a more specific dashboard (per-endpoint latency, dependency latency) for diagnosis. The golden dashboard is canonical because it is the minimal sufficient view for triage.

**Visual:**
```
Golden Signals Dashboard (templated by $service):

  [Latency p99: 245ms]  [Req/s: 1.2k]  [Err rate: 0.3%]  [CPU: 73%]
   (green)              (green)         (yellow)           (green)
  -----------------------------------------------------------------
  Latency p99 over 1h    |  Throughput over 1h
  (line chart)           |  (line chart)
  -----------------------------------------------------------------
  Error rate over 1h     |  CPU/Mem over 1h
  (line chart)           |  (line chart)
  -----------------------------------------------------------------
  Error logs (last 1h, filtered to ERROR)
  (log stream)
```

sections.title: Scenario-Based Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. Your team has 200 dashboards in Grafana, half of which are stale or broken. How do you clean this up?
**Answer:** Dashboard sprawl is the most common Grafana anti-pattern — engineers create dashboards for one-off investigations, never delete them, and they accumulate until no one trusts any of them. The cleanup is a quarterly exercise. First, instrument dashboard usage: Grafana logs every dashboard view (or you can use the Grafana audit log or the `dashboard_views` metric in Grafana Enterprise); dashboards not viewed in 90 days are candidates for deletion. Second, classify each dashboard: "operational" (used in incident response, kept), "exploration" (one-off investigation, archive or delete), "reporting" (used by stakeholders, kept but reviewed for accuracy). Third, for each kept dashboard, verify queries work (Grafana's "test query" feature) — broken queries usually mean the underlying metric was renamed or deleted, and the dashboard must be updated or deleted. Fourth, consolidate: many teams have 5 dashboards that all show the same service from slightly different angles — merge into one templated dashboard. Fifth, adopt provisioning: move all kept dashboards to a Git repo, delete from the database, and reload from Git so future changes go through PR review. Sixth, set a policy: every new dashboard must have an owner (a team label) and a TTL (delete after 90 days unless promoted to operational). Real-world: Grafana Labs themselves run this exercise quarterly and report 30–50% dashboard reduction each time.

**Visual:**
```
Audit:
  1. usage log: views in last 90d -> 100 unused
  2. classify: operational / exploration / reporting
  3. test queries: 50 broken (renamed metrics)
  4. consolidate: 5 per-service dashboards -> 1 templated
  5. provision to Git, delete from DB
  6. policy: owner + TTL on every new dashboard

Result: 200 dashboards -> 80 trusted, version-controlled
```

### Q2. You want to set up cross-panel drill-down: clicking a point on a latency chart filters a log panel to that time and service. How do you build this in Grafana?
**Answer:** Grafana's "data links" feature lets you configure a link on any panel that navigates to another dashboard (or external URL) with variables populated from the clicked point. Step one: ensure both dashboards share the same templating variables (`$service`, `$env`, `$__time_range`). Step two: on the latency panel, configure a data link with URL `/d/log-dashboard?var-service=${__field.labels.service}&from=${__value.time}&to=${__value.time+300000}` — this passes the clicked series's `service` label and the clicked point's timestamp (plus 5 minutes) to the log dashboard's variables. Step three: in the log dashboard, the `$service` variable and the dashboard time range filter the Loki query (`{service="$service"}`), so opening the link shows logs for the same service in the same time window. Step four: for in-dashboard drill-down (no navigation), use Grafana's "shared crosshair" (a vertical line across all time-series panels synced to the mouse position) and "shared tooltip" so the engineer sees all panels' values at the same timestamp. Step five: for log-to-trace drill-down, configure the Loki panel's data link to extract the `trace_id` field from the clicked log line and navigate to Tempo with `trace_id` as a query parameter. This is the "three pillars in one UI" workflow Grafana Labs sells.

**Visual:**
```
Latency panel:
  click point at t=14:23:01 on series service=checkout
  -> data link: /d/log-db?var-service=checkout&from=14:23:01&to=14:28:01

Log dashboard (receives link):
  $service = checkout
  $__time_range = 14:23:01 to 14:28:01
  Loki query: {service="checkout"} (filtered to 5-min window)

Click log line -> extract trace_id -> navigate to Tempo
```

### Q3. Your team wants to provision 50 dashboards from Git. How do you set up the pipeline?
**Answer:** The pipeline has four components: the Git repo, the CI/CD system, the Grafana instance, and the provisioning directory. Step one: create a Git repo with structure `dashboards/*.json` (one file per dashboard, exported from Grafana as JSON), `datasources/*.yaml`, `alerting/*.yaml`, and a `README` documenting the convention. Step two: in the Grafana instance, configure provisioning by adding to `grafana.ini` or environment variables: `GF_PATHS_PROVISIONING=/etc/grafana/provisioning`, and mount the provisioned directory from a ConfigMap (Kubernetes) or volume. Step three: in CI/CD (GitHub Actions, GitLab CI), add a job that on every push to `main` syncs the repo to the Grafana instance — for Kubernetes, this rebuilds the ConfigMap and triggers a rolling restart of Grafana; for VMs, this rsyncs the files and Grafana's file watcher reloads automatically. Step four: dashboard JSON must be exported with the "Export for sharing externally" option checked (no internal IDs) so the same JSON works across staging and prod. Step five: the Grafana Terraform provider is an alternative for managing dashboards, folders, permissions, and data sources as code, useful if you also need to manage Grafana's own configuration. Step six: PR review policy — every dashboard change is a JSON diff in a PR, reviewed by another engineer, just like code. Real-world: Grafana Labs runs this internally and publishes their dashboards as open-source for customers to fork.

**Visual:**
```
Git repo:                CI/CD:                   Grafana:
  dashboards/              on push to main:        GF_PATHS_PROVISIONING=
    svc-overview.json        - validate JSON         /etc/grafana/provisioning/
    svc-deepdive.json        - sync to grafana           dashboards/*.json
  datasources/                - k8s: update              datasources/*.yaml
    prom.yaml                   ConfigMap +                alerting/*.yaml
    loki.yaml                   rolling restart        (file watcher reloads)
  alerting/
    high-err.yaml        PR review on every change
```

### Q4. A stakeholder wants a dashboard showing daily revenue, but the data is in PostgreSQL. How do you build this in Grafana?
**Answer:** Grafana's PostgreSQL data source plugin lets you query Postgres directly from a Grafana panel. Step one: install the Postgres data source plugin (built-in in recent Grafana versions) and configure a connection — host, port, database, user (read-only, with `GRANT SELECT ON revenue TO grafana_reader`), TLS, and connection pool settings. Step two: in the dashboard, add a panel with the Postgres data source and write SQL that respects Grafana's time-range variable: `SELECT date_trunc('day', created_at) AS time, SUM(amount) AS revenue FROM orders WHERE created_at BETWEEN $__timeFrom() AND $__timeTo() GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1`. The `$__timeFrom()` and `$__timeTo()` macros are substituted with the dashboard's time range, so the same query works for "last 7 days" and "last 30 days." Step three: use the bar chart panel type for daily revenue (one bar per day), with the y-axis unit set to currency (`prefix: $`). Step four: add a templating variable `$region` populated by `SELECT DISTINCT region FROM orders` so the stakeholder can filter by region. Step five: schedule the dashboard as a Grafana report (Grafana Enterprise feature) — Grafana renders the dashboard to PDF and emails it daily at 9 AM. Step six: for sub-second queries on large tables, add an index on `created_at` and consider a materialized view refreshed nightly. Real-world: hedge funds use this pattern for daily P&L dashboards.

**Visual:**
```
Postgres data source:
  host=db.internal:5432, user=grafana_reader (read-only)
  GRANT SELECT ON orders TO grafana_reader

Panel query (bar chart, currency):
  SELECT date_trunc('day', created_at) AS time,
         SUM(amount) AS revenue
  FROM orders
  WHERE created_at BETWEEN $__timeFrom() AND $__timeTo()
    AND region = '$region'
  GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1

+ Grafana Enterprise: schedule daily PDF report at 9 AM
```

### Q5. Your Prometheus queries are slow (10+ seconds) on a Grafana dashboard. How do you diagnose and fix this?
**Answer:** Slow PromQL queries in Grafana have three common causes: high cardinality, expensive aggregations, or excessive time range. Step one: identify the slow query — open the dashboard, open the browser's network tab, find the slowest `/api/ds/query` request, and copy the PromQL. Step two: run `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` equivalent — Prometheus does not have this directly, but you can use the Prometheus UI's query inspector or check `prometheus_engine_query_duration_seconds` to see how long the query took on the server. Step three: check cardinality — if the query selects many series (`http_requests_total` without filters selects all), the response is huge; add label filters (`{job="checkout"}`) to narrow it. Step four: check the aggregation — `sum(rate(...)) by (everything)` is expensive; reduce the `by` clause to only the labels you actually chart. Step five: check the time range — a 30-day query at 15-second resolution is 170K samples per series, multiplied by N series; use `$__interval` (auto-binning based on time range) instead of fixed `[5m]` so a 30-day query uses 1-hour bins. Step six: check for `rate()` over too-short a window — `rate(...[1m])` on a 15-second scrape interval only has 4 samples, noisy and slow; use at least `[5m]`. Step seven: if the query is inherently expensive (large `histogram_quantile` over many series), pre-compute it with a recording rule (`RECORD checkout:p99_latency = histogram_quantile(...)`) so the dashboard queries the pre-computed series. Step eight: if Prometheus itself is the bottleneck (slow disk, high cardinality), migrate to Mimir for horizontal scalability.

**Visual:**
```
Diagnose:
  1. browser network tab -> slowest /api/ds/query
  2. copy PromQL, check prometheus_engine_query_duration_seconds
  3. high cardinality? add label filters
  4. expensive aggregation? reduce by() clause
  5. long time range? use $__interval (auto-bin)
  6. rate over [1m]? -> [5m] minimum
  7. expensive histogram_quantile? -> recording rule
  8. Prometheus itself slow? -> Mimir
```

### Q6. Your team wants to migrate from Kibana to Grafana Loki for logs. How do you architect the migration?
**Answer:** The migration is a phased cutover, not a big-bang switch, because logs are critical for incident response and any gap is risky. Phase one (parallel ingestion): deploy Loki alongside Elasticsearch, and configure the log shipper (Fluent Bit, Vector) to write to both — this lets you compare query results and verify Loki is capturing everything Elasticsearch is. Phase two (parallel query): deploy Grafana with both Loki and Elasticsearch as data sources, so engineers can query either; build Grafana dashboards that use Loki for new investigations and keep Elasticsearch available for historical queries. Phase three (cutover for new logs): after 30 days of parallel ingestion, switch the shipper to write to Loki only (with a fallback to Elasticsearch if Loki is down), so new logs go to Loki and old logs remain in Elasticsearch until they age out. Phase four (decommission Elasticsearch): once the Elasticsearch retention window (e.g., 30 days) has elapsed, all logs are in Loki; decommission the Elasticsearch cluster. Phase five (cost optimization): with Loki's label-only indexing, query patterns shift — engineers must know which service and time window to investigate (label-based), not search full-text across all logs. Train the team on LogQL (`{service="checkout"} |= "ERROR" | json | latency > 1`). The expected outcome is 10–100x cost reduction (Loki stores compressed chunks in S3, no full-text index), with the trade-off of slower ad-hoc substring search across unknown fields.

**Visual:**
```
Phase 1 (parallel ingest):  shipper -> ES + Loki (30d)
Phase 2 (parallel query):   Grafana queries both
Phase 3 (Loki only):        shipper -> Loki (ES ages out)
Phase 4 (decommission ES):  after retention window
Phase 5 (cost optimization): train team on LogQL label-based queries

Result: 10-100x cost reduction (S3 chunks vs. ES full-text index)
Trade-off: slower ad-hoc substring across unknown fields
```

### Q7. You are designing a multi-tenant Grafana for 20 teams. How do you isolate teams while sharing infrastructure?
**Answer:** Multi-tenant Grafana has three isolation layers: data, dashboard, and access. Data isolation: each team's metrics go to a separate Mimir tenant (`X-Scope-OrgID: team-a`), so team A cannot query team B's metrics even if they have the dashboard. Dashboard isolation: Grafana folders are per-team, with folder-level permissions (`team-a` folder is editable only by `team-a` group), so each team owns its dashboards. Access isolation: Grafana's RBAC (or Grafana Enterprise's team-based permissions) controls who can view, edit, and admin each folder and dashboard. The architecture: one Grafana instance (or HA pair) serves all teams; each team has its own folder tree (`team-a/operations`, `team-a/investigation`, `team-a/reporting`); data sources are either shared (one Mimir with per-team tenant header passed via Grafana's data source proxy) or per-team (one Mimir tenant per data source). Templating variables scoped to the team (`$team` is read-only, set to the user's team). For stricter isolation (compliance, security), use separate Grafana instances per team — this is more expensive but provides hard isolation. The trade-off is operational efficiency (one Grafana is cheaper to run and upgrade) versus isolation (separate Grafanas provide hard boundaries). Real-world: Grafana Cloud's multi-tenant SaaS uses per-tenant Mimir tenants with a shared Grafana UI; large enterprises with compliance requirements often run separate Grafanas per business unit.

**Visual:**
```
Multi-tenant Grafana (one instance, 20 teams):

  Folder: /team-a/      <- RBAC: team-a group can edit
    operations.json
    investigation.json
  Folder: /team-b/      <- RBAC: team-b group can edit
    operations.json

  Data source: Mimir
    team-a panel -> header X-Scope-OrgID: team-a
    team-b panel -> header X-Scope-OrgID: team-b

  Templating: $team is read-only (set from user's group)

Stricter isolation (separate instances, e.g. for compliance):
  team-a.grafana.corp  -> Mimir tenant team-a
  team-b.grafana.corp  -> Mimir tenant team-b
```

quiz.explanation: Grafana alerting, introduced in v8 (2021) and unified in v9, lets users define alert rules that query any data source (Prometheus, Loki, MySQL, CloudWatch), evaluate on a schedule, and route to notification channels. Prometheus alerting is built into Prometheus itself: alert rules are written in PromQL, evaluated by Prometheus, and routed to Alertmanager for dedup, grouping, and notification.
